title: The Effect of Strength Training Methods on Middle-Distance and Long-Distance Runners' Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
authors: Llanos-Lagos C, Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Saez de Villarreal E
population: Middle- and long-distance runners of any sex and level (324 moderately trained, 272 well trained, 298 highly trained athletes); randomized and non-randomized controlled studies; programs of 6-40 weeks with 1-4 sessions per week
findings: Certainty of evidence was very low to moderate (GRADE); search through November 2022.

High-load training improved running performance (time trial or time to exhaustion) with a moderate effect (ES -0.469, p = 0.029); combined methods had a large effect (ES -1.035, p = 0.036); plyometric training alone was not significant (ES -0.210, p = 0.064).
No method improved VO2max, vVO2max, maximum metabolic steady state or sprint capacity (all p > 0.072).

Moderators (sex, age, body mass, height, VO2max, performance level, strength training experience, weeks, sessions per week, total sessions) had no effect on running performance variables or determinants (all p > 0.166).
limitations: Very low to moderate certainty; the large combined-methods effect rests on few studies; non-significant moderators may reflect low power rather than true absence of dose effects; time trial and time-to-exhaustion tests are pooled. Sample size is the sum of the three athlete-level counts; overlaps with the economy review.
implications: Credit strength work with a performance benefit through economy and neuromuscular factors, not VO2max or threshold; derive VO2max and threshold estimates from running data only.
Because no dose moderator was detected, 2 sessions per week is a justified default and frequency should not be escalated to chase more benefit.
Combine heavy and plyometric work in the same block where tolerated.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC re-fetched; all numbers in abstract. Added 'height' to the moderator list per abstract.
